messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 53-year-old bus driver, had always prided himself on his steady reliability and his easygoing manner with passengers. Life with his wife was comfortable, if sometimes routine, and he found satisfaction in the rhythm of his daily routes. But everything fractured one late autumn night, about two years ago. He had offered a ride home to a stranded acquaintance after a community event, taking a detour through an unfamiliar part of town. Tired after a long day, he hadn't noticed the subtle shift in the man's demeanor until it was too late. The assault occurred in the isolated alley where he’d stopped, the muffled sounds of the city providing an eerie soundtrack to the terrifying event.

In the months that followed, Mark found his world shrinking. The memories were merciless. His memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over in his mind, often without warning. When he remembered the event, he felt an intense shame, not just for what had happened, but for how it had stripped him of his sense of self. Remembering the event often brought back the same terror he felt at the time, a visceral re-experiencing that left him breathless and disoriented. This relentless replay of the event, a film he couldn't stop watching, kept the details so vivid and raw that the slightest echo of the night, a particular sound or the sensation of fatigue, was enough to instantly pull him back into the nightmare, making these cues potent triggers.

His occupation, once a source of stability, became a minefield. Mark found that feeling very tired or exhausted, a common state after long shifts, would often be the first crack in his composure. When the familiar hum of the bus engine would hit a certain pitch, or a passenger's voice carried a particular tone, Mark would suddenly find himself back in that alley, the terror of the attack engulfing him once more. Driving with people, especially when his bus was full, became a constant ordeal. Each time he felt himself grow weary on a long route, a profound sense of despair would wash over him, solidifying his belief that he had truly lost his faith in the fundamental goodness of life. He had come to believe that people couldn't be trusted, a conviction that gnawed at him daily.

Because he had come to believe that people couldn't be trusted, Mark found himself constantly on edge, scrutinizing every passenger, every sound, which in turn made him hyper-sensitive to the very cues that would drag him back into the past. His deep-seated mistrust of others made the memories of the assault particularly agonizing, each replay confirming his conviction that people were inherently dangerous, and intensifying the shame he felt about what had happened to his body. He felt a profound sense of body shame, a quiet horror at the violation, which made him recoil from intimacy with his wife and avoid looking at himself in the mirror. This pervasive sense of mistrust and shame kept the memories fresh and terrifying, creating a vicious cycle where the constant reliving of the event fueled his conviction that the world was a dangerous place and he himself was tainted.

The strain of managing these internal battles had begun to take a toll on his work performance and his marriage. He started calling in sick more often, citing vague illnesses, and his once easy banter with colleagues had vanished. At home, he was distant, preoccupied, and irritable. His wife, worried and confused, finally urged him to seek help. Mark came to therapy feeling utterly defeated, exhausted by the ceaseless internal battle, and desperately hoping for some relief from the terror and shame that had consumed his life, but secretly convinced that no one could truly understand or help him reclaim the trust he had lost.
